components.name: Oysters Rockefeller, born at Antoine’s
components.explain:
Oysters Rockefeller was created at Antoine's in the French Quarter, around 1899 by most accounts, and is credited to Jules Alciatore, son of the founder. The usual story is that local oysters took the place of snails that were hard to import. The dish was named for John D. Rockefeller, the richest American of the day, for the richness of its green sauce. The classic is oysters on the half shell under that sauce and breadcrumbs, baked or broiled.

Antoine's keeps its recipe secret and has long said it holds no spinach; most cooks since have used spinach.

Our Rockefeller Gratin is the Thanksgiving Day version: oysters, bacon, creamed spinach and breadcrumbs baked as a gratin. Say it is our take on the classic, not Antoine's recipe.

card.front: Where and when was oysters Rockefeller created?
card.back: At Antoine's in the French Quarter, around 1899 by most accounts, credited to Jules Alciatore and named for John D. Rockefeller for its rich green sauce.

components.name: Gratin, the browned crust
components.explain:
A gratin is a dish baked or grilled until a browned crust forms on top, most often of breadcrumbs, cheese or both. The word comes from the French gratter, to scrape: it first named the crust that stuck to the pot and was scraped off, and only later the dish with a deliberate crust. Au gratin does not mean with cheese, whatever many menus suggest.

The crust is the point: crunch and toasted flavour over something soft and rich underneath.

On the Rockefeller Gratin the breadcrumbs bake into that crust over oysters, bacon and creamed spinach. How long and how hot the kitchen bakes it is a lineup question.

card.front: What does gratin mean, and does it mean cheese?
card.back: From the French gratter, to scrape: a dish baked until a browned crust forms on top, often breadcrumbs. Au gratin does not mean with cheese.

components.name: Belgian endive
components.explain:
Belgian endive is chicory grown twice: the roots are lifted and forced again in the dark, so the new leaves grow into a tight, pale spear, crisp and only gently bitter. Light turns them green and much more bitter, which is why it is grown and stored in the dark. The Flemish call it witloof, white leaf; it was developed around Brussels in the 1830s.

Curly endive, or frisée, is a different chicory with ragged green leaves and a sharper bite; both belong to the chicory family, and a menu that says endive can mean either.

The Endive Satsuma Salad prints endive and no more, so confirm at lineup which one the kitchen uses before describing the leaf to a guest.

card.front: Why is Belgian endive pale and only gently bitter?
card.back: It is chicory forced from the root in the dark, so the leaves stay white, tight and mild; light turns them green and bitter. The Flemish call it witloof.

components.name: Satsuma
components.explain:
The satsuma is a mandarin, Citrus unshiu, first recorded in Japan centuries ago and named in the West for the old Satsuma province, now Kagoshima. It reached the United States in the 1870s. It is usually seedless, with a loose skin that peels easily, and sweet, mild segments.

In Louisiana it is the main citrus: satsumas are most of the state's citrus acreage, and Plaquemines Parish is the centre of the crop. They ripen in the autumn, from about October into December, and growers say colour is no sure sign of sweetness.

The Endive Satsuma Salad sets the fruit against bitter endive and a cherry vinaigrette. The sheet does not say whether the satsumas are local, so ask before calling them Louisiana fruit.

card.front: What is a satsuma, and where does Louisiana grow it?
card.back: A sweet, usually seedless, easy peeling mandarin named for Japan's Satsuma province; Louisiana's main citrus, centred in Plaquemines Parish and harvested from about October into December.

components.name: Roasted sunflower seeds
components.explain:
Sunflower seeds are the kernels of Helianthus annuus, a plant native to North America and domesticated in its east long before Europeans arrived. Roasted, they turn golden and taste nutty and toasty, with a soft crunch rather than the hard snap of an almond.

On a salad they do the job croutons or nuts would do: texture and a savoury, toasted note against soft leaves and a sharp dressing.

The Endive Satsuma Salad prints roasted sunflower seeds, though the photograph cuts that line at the page edge, so confirm the wording at lineup. Whether they are salted, seasoned or candied is the kitchen's to say, and seed questions always go to the kitchen.

card.front: What do the roasted sunflower seeds bring to the endive salad?
card.back: Toasty, nutty crunch against soft leaves and a sharp dressing. The sunflower is native to North America; how ours are seasoned is a question for the kitchen.

components.name: Louisiana sweet potatoes
components.explain:
Louisiana growers began calling their moist, orange sweet potatoes yams to set them apart from the drier kinds grown further east; the LSU AgCenter dates the name to the 1930s and calls yam the trademark of the Louisiana sweet potato. Botanically it is no yam at all: a true yam belongs to a different plant family.

The Beauregard, released by the LSU AgCenter in 1987, became an industry standard across the United States, an orange-fleshed variety.

On Thanksgiving Day the sweet potato appears twice: inside the Sweet Potato Agnolotti, as the name says, and in the Sweet Potato Pot de Crème. The sheet does not say where the potatoes are from, so ask before calling them Louisiana grown.

card.front: Why do Louisianans call sweet potatoes yams?
card.back: A marketing name from the 1930s to set the moist, orange Louisiana sweet potato apart; botanically it is no yam. The Beauregard, from the LSU AgCenter in 1987, became an industry standard.

components.name: Agnolotti, the folded pasta
components.explain:
Agnolotti are a filled pasta of Piedmont in northwest Italy. Ravioli are two pieces of pasta sealed around a filling; agnolotti are made from one piece folded over it and pressed shut, so each parcel has a fold on one side. The small pinched kind is agnolotti del plin. Where the name comes from is not settled.

The pinched agnolotti del plin are the miniature form, normally about three centimetres across, and plin means pinched.

Our fall menu's Agnolotti del Plin are the pinched kind with pork; the Thanksgiving Day Sweet Potato Agnolotti are filled, as the name says, with sweet potato, finished in brown butter with candied pecans and chèvre. Do not mix the two up at the table.

card.front: How do agnolotti differ from ravioli?
card.back: Ravioli are two sheets sealed around a filling; agnolotti, from Piedmont, are one sheet folded over it. Our Thanksgiving agnolotti hold sweet potato.

components.name: Chèvre
components.explain:
Chèvre is the French word for goat, short for fromage de chèvre, goat cheese. In English it usually means the fresh, soft kind: white, creamy and tangy, with a clean, lactic sourness that cuts through sweet and rich food.

Fresh chèvre crumbles or spreads; aged goat cheeses grow firmer and stronger, but a menu that says chèvre most often means the fresh one.

On the Sweet Potato Agnolotti the chèvre's tang balances the sweet potato, the brown butter and the candied pecans. The sheet does not say whether it is in the filling or on top, or which cheese it is, so confirm at lineup; any question about dairy or what is in the cheese goes to the kitchen.

card.front: What is chèvre, and what does it do on the agnolotti?
card.back: French for goat: here fresh goat cheese, soft and tangy. Its tang balances the sweet potato, brown butter and candied pecans; where it sits is a lineup question.

components.name: Bay scallops, served raw
components.explain:
Bay scallops are the small scallops of shallow bays and estuaries, half an inch to an inch across and often seventy to a hundred or more to the pound. Sea scallops come from deeper water, larger, often ten to thirty to the pound. Bay scallops are the sweeter and more tender; sea scallops are firmer and chewier. What a guest eats is the adductor, the round muscle that closes the shell.

Under the FDA Food Code a scallop served as the shucked adductor muscle alone is exempt from the parasite freezing most raw fish needs, as oysters are; the consumer advisory for raw food still applies.

On the Bay Scallop Crudo they are served raw. Where tonight's scallops come from, and the advisory wording the house wants, are lineup questions.

card.front: How do bay scallops differ from sea scallops?
card.back: Bay scallops are small, half an inch to an inch across, from shallow bays, sweeter and more tender; sea scallops are larger, from deeper water, firmer. Ours are served raw, with the advisory.

components.name: Meyer lemon
components.explain:
The Meyer lemon came to the United States in 1908, collected near Peking by Frank N. Meyer, a USDA plant explorer, and it carries his name. It is deep yellow with an orange tint when ripe, thin skinned and juicy, and sweeter and less acidic than a common Eureka or Lisbon lemon. Long called a cross of lemon and mandarin, it is now thought to descend from citron, mandarin and pummelo.

Less sharp than a common lemon, it brightens delicate food with less sourness.

On the Bay Scallop Crudo it brightens raw scallops gently. Whether the kitchen uses juice, zest or segments is a lineup question.

card.front: What makes a Meyer lemon different from a common lemon?
card.back: It is sweeter and less acidic, deep yellow and thin skinned; brought from near Peking in 1908 by Frank N. Meyer, a USDA plant explorer.

components.name: Black truffle
components.explain:
The black Périgord truffle, Tuber melanosporum, is the winter truffle of south west France and Spain, dug from about mid-November to mid-March with dogs or pigs, and prized above all for its aroma, earthy and savoury. A cheaper winter truffle, the brumale, grows in the same soils and is often confused with it.

Truffles grow underground and are found by scent, and their aroma changes as they are stored, which is why a guest may ask whether one is fresh.

The Bay Scallop Crudo prints black truffle, cut at the page edge. Which truffle it is, fresh or preserved, is the kitchen's answer: do not promise a fresh Périgord truffle until you know.

card.front: What is the black Périgord truffle, and when is it in season?
card.back: Tuber melanosporum, a winter truffle dug from about mid-November to mid-March, valued for its earthy aroma. Which truffle the crudo carries, fresh or preserved, is a lineup question.

components.name: Radish
components.explain:
The radish is a root of the mustard family, crisp, juicy and cool, with a peppery bite. The bite is not in the intact root: when it is cut or chewed, glucosinolates and an enzyme stored apart in its cells meet and form isothiocyanates, the same mustard oils that give mustard, horseradish and wasabi their heat.

The plant makes these compounds to keep fungi and grazing animals away; to a cook they are simply the pepper.

On the Bay Scallop Crudo the radish gives crunch and a little pepper against the soft, sweet scallop and the citrus. How it is cut, and which radish, are the kitchen's to tell you at lineup.

card.front: Where does a radish get its peppery bite?
card.back: Cutting or chewing mixes glucosinolates with an enzyme, forming mustard oils, the same heat as mustard and horseradish. On the crudo it adds crunch and pepper.

components.name: Pot de crème, the custard in its pot
components.explain:
Pot de crème is French for pot of cream, the cream meaning custard: a loose custard of cream, milk and egg yolks, baked gently until just set, usually in a water bath, and served in the small pot or ramekin it was baked in. It is soft and spoonable.

The gentle heat is the craft: too hot and the custard curdles into grains and weeps.

The Thanksgiving Day Sweet Potato Pot de Crème is made with sweet potato, miso, cinnamon and marshmallow fluff. The sheet prints no method, so ask the kitchen how it is set before you describe it.

card.front: What is a pot de crème?
card.back: French for pot of cream: a silky custard baked gently, usually in a water bath, and served in the little pot it set in. Ours is sweet potato.

components.name: Miso in a dessert
components.explain:
Miso is a Japanese paste of soybeans fermented with salt and koji. In a dessert it does what salt does in salted caramel: a little brings savoury depth and makes the sweetness taste rounder and less flat. White, or shiro, miso is the mildest and sweetest and the usual choice; pastry cooks warn that too much overwhelms a sweet dish. Miso caramel is the most common form.

The soybeans make it a soy question every time, and those questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

On the Sweet Potato Pot de Crème the miso sits with sweet potato, cinnamon and marshmallow. Which miso, and whether it is in the custard or a caramel, is the kitchen's to say.

card.front: Why would a pastry cook put miso in a dessert?
card.back: For salt and savoury depth, the way salted caramel works: it makes sweetness taste rounder. White miso is the usual choice. Soy questions go to the kitchen.

components.name: Marshmallow Fluff
components.explain:
Marshmallow Fluff is a marshmallow creme, a soft, spoonable whipped marshmallow sold in jars. The recipe was first sold door to door in Somerville, Massachusetts, and bought by two candy makers of Lynn, H. Allen Durkee and Fred Mower, whose firm, Durkee-Mower, still makes it in Lynn; their partnership dates to 1920.

It is sweet, sticky and light, and it browns under heat like a marshmallow.

The Sweet Potato Pot de Crème prints marshmallow fluff, a nod to the sweet potato and marshmallow casserole. Whether the kitchen uses the jarred brand or its own whipped marshmallow, and whether it is toasted, are lineup questions; questions about what is in it go to the kitchen.

card.front: What is Marshmallow Fluff?
card.back: A marshmallow creme, soft whipped marshmallow in a jar, made by Durkee-Mower in Lynn, Massachusetts. Whether ours is the brand or house made is a lineup question.

components.name: Marshmallows on sweet potatoes
components.explain:
The first documented recipe for mashed sweet potatoes baked under a marshmallow topping appeared in 1917, in a recipe booklet the Angelus Marshmallow company commissioned from Janet McKenzie Hill of the Boston Cooking School Magazine. The aim was to sell more marshmallows by making them an everyday ingredient, and it worked: Angelus, later Campfire, printed more sweet potato and marshmallow recipes around 1930.

The casserole spread from there to holiday tables across the country, which is why guests smile when they read marshmallow beside sweet potato.

The Sweet Potato Pot de Crème turns that casserole into a French custard: sweet potato, cinnamon, miso and marshmallow fluff. It is a story worth one line at the table.

card.front: Where does marshmallow on sweet potato come from?
card.back: A 1917 recipe booklet the Angelus Marshmallow company commissioned to sell marshmallows printed the first documented recipe; the casserole became a Thanksgiving habit. Our pot de crème recalls it.

components.name: Chocolate and orange
components.explain:
Chocolate and orange is an old partnership of the confectioner's shop. Orangettes, strips of orange peel candied slowly and coated in a thin layer of dark chocolate, are its classic form, and chocolatiers describe the appeal as two contrasting tastes, one full bodied and one tangy.

The reason it works is contrast: tangy, slightly bitter citrus against full bodied cocoa, so each makes the other taste brighter.

On the Chocolate and Orange Tart the pair is set in a tart with candied hazelnuts for crunch. The sheet does not say where the orange sits, in the filling, the crust or a garnish, so ask the kitchen at lineup.

card.front: Why do chocolate and orange go together?
card.back: Bright, slightly bitter citrus cuts the weight of cocoa butter, so chocolate tastes deeper and lighter; orangettes, candied peel in dark chocolate, are the classic form.

components.name: Stuffing and dressing
components.explain:
Stuffing and dressing are the same family of dish, bread or another starch mixed with fat, aromatics and stock. By the usual rule, stuffing is cooked inside the bird and dressing in its own pan, though many cooks use the words for either. In the South, dressing is the common word however it is cooked, and Southern dressing is often made with cornbread.

Food safety guidance asks for 165°F in the centre, whether it is cooked in the bird or in a pan.

On Thanksgiving Day the turkey comes with its own cornbread dressing, and Titus' BBQ Shrimp Stuffing is a side for the table that carries New Orleans BBQ shrimp. What it is built on is a lineup question.

card.front: What is the difference between stuffing and dressing?
card.back: By the usual rule, stuffing cooks inside the bird and dressing in a pan; in the South dressing is the common word either way, often made with cornbread.

components.name: The herbed potato purée, a side for the table
components.explain:
Pommes purée is the French potato purée, smoother and denser than an everyday mash. The cooked potatoes are pressed through a ricer or a food mill, or in the old way passed through a fine drum sieve called a tamis, and then a generous share of butter and cream is worked in until it is silky. It is pressed, not beaten, because overworked potato turns gluey.

So the texture is the test: smooth, glossy and spoonable rather than fluffy.

On Thanksgiving Day the Herbed Potato Purée is a side for the table, and the beef tenderloin comes with its own pommes purée. Whether they are the same, and which herbs go in, are lineup questions.

card.front: How is the herbed potato purée side unlike everyday mash?
card.back: The potatoes are pressed through a ricer, food mill or tamis, never beaten, and enriched with plenty of butter and cream, so the purée is silky and dense.

components.name: Haricots verts
components.explain:
Haricots verts is French for green beans, and on an American menu the words name the thin, slender French type, picked young while the pod is tender and the seeds inside are small. They are the young pods of the common bean, a plant that came to the world's kitchens from Mexico and the Andes.

They cook in minutes: blanched in salted water and shocked in iced water, then finished in butter or a hot pan, they stay bright green with a snap, and cooked long they turn soft and olive coloured.

On Thanksgiving Day they are a $7 side for the table, the green that lightens a plate of turkey, purée and stuffing. How the kitchen finishes them is a lineup question.

card.front: What are haricots verts?
card.back: French for green beans: the thin, slender French type, picked young. Cooked briefly they stay bright and crisp; on Thanksgiving Day they are a $7 side for the table.

components.name: Cranberries
components.explain:
The American cranberry, Vaccinium macrocarpon, is native to the bogs and wetlands of central and eastern North America, and Native peoples gathered it long before colonists came. At harvest, growers flood the bogs and the berries, which hold pockets of air, float to the surface to be gathered. The berries ripen from mid-September to mid-November, so they are in season for Thanksgiving, although the record does not show them at the first feast.

Raw they are sharply sour; cooked with sugar they make a sauce that is tart, bright and sweet.

On Thanksgiving Day the Cranberry Sauce is a $7 side for the table, and the turkey's jus carries cranberry too. How the house makes its sauce is a lineup question.

card.front: Why are cranberries on the Thanksgiving table?
card.back: They are native to North American bogs and ripen from mid-September to mid-November, in season for the holiday; cooked with sugar, their sharp acid cuts rich turkey.

entries.label: Oysters Rockefeller, the classic
entries.same: Oysters baked under a rich green layer and breadcrumbs until hot and browned.
entries.different: The classic is on the half shell under a secret green sauce; ours is a gratin of oysters, bacon and creamed spinach.

entries.label: A salad with cherries
entries.same: Crisp leaves with cherry for sweet and tart fruit and something toasty for crunch.
entries.different: Ours sets gently bitter endive against sweet satsuma, with the cherry in the vinaigrette and roasted sunflower seeds.

entries.label: Piedmont’s pinched filled pasta
entries.same: A filled egg pasta from Piedmont, sealed by hand around a soft filling and finished simply.
entries.different: Ours is folded around sweet potato and finished with brown butter, candied pecans and chèvre.

entries.label: A raw geoduck crudo
entries.same: Raw seafood sliced and dressed at the last moment with citrus, served cold.
entries.different: Ours is small, sweet bay scallops with Meyer lemon, black truffle and radish.

entries.label: Crème brûlée, the burnt cream
entries.same: A baked cream and egg custard set gently and served in its own dish.
entries.different: Ours is sweet potato with miso, cinnamon and marshmallow fluff, and no burnt sugar crust.

entries.label: Orangettes
entries.same: Chocolate and orange together, the citrus cutting the richness of cocoa.
entries.different: Ours is a tart, with candied hazelnuts for crunch; orangettes are candied peel dipped in dark chocolate.

entries.label: New Orleans BBQ shrimp
entries.same: Shrimp in the buttery, peppery New Orleans BBQ style, never grilled or smoked.
entries.different: Ours folds that style into a holiday stuffing, a side for the table.

entries.label: Mashing and puréeing potatoes
entries.same: Cooked potato pressed smooth and enriched with butter and cream.
entries.different: Ours is herbed, a side for the Thanksgiving table; which herbs is a lineup question.

entries.label: The green bean casserole
entries.same: Green beans on the Thanksgiving table beside the turkey.
entries.different: Ours are thin French beans cooked briefly to stay bright and crisp, not baked in a creamy sauce.

entries.label: A Cape Cod cranberry relish
entries.same: Tart cranberries sweetened for the holiday table, a bright foil for turkey.
entries.different: Ours is a cooked sauce, a $7 side for the table; how it is made is a lineup question.
